The Sompat grunt attains a maximum recorded total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a size that positions it as one of the larger members within the Haemulidae family in West African coastal waters. While a significant portion of the population does not reach this extreme, these values are derived from extensive commercial catch surveys. During the course of their development, individuals undergo a pronounced shift in morphology and ecology, progressing from a pelagic larval stage to a demersal juvenile existence before reaching adulthood. The transition to a reproductively active state is marked by the onset of gonadal maturation, which in this species occurs when individuals have achieved a total length of 13.1 centimeters [Lp = 13.1 centimeters]. This length at puberty is relatively modest compared to the species' ultimate size, ensuring that reproductive capacity is established well before the individual has completed its somatic growth. Early maturation is a common trait among tropical marine fishes, allowing them to exploit favorable environmental conditions for spawning before the risks of high adult mortality take their toll.

Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae of the Sompat grunt possess a remarkably small wet weight at birth of 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value reflecting the minute size of the pelagic egg from which they hatch. This initial mass is derived from morphometric relationships based on an average egg diameter, placing the species among marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small offspring. Following eclosion, the non-feeding larva relies entirely on its yolk reserves to sustain its rapid development and early growth. The period of endotrophic existence is brief, with hatching occurring after approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] when eggs are incubated at a stable temperature of 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C]. This rapid pace of embryonic development is typical for warm-water lutjanid and haemulid species, where elevated temperatures accelerate the metabolic processes governing cellular differentiation. The larvae then transition to an exotrophic mode, commencing first feeding on planktonic prey as their mouth gapes become functional.

As the Sompat grunt progresses through its juvenile and adult phases, its body mass increases substantially from the larval stage. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult can reach 2746 grams [Wwi = can reach 2746 grams], a value derived from a robust length-weight relationship established from a large sample of individuals across its geographic range. This asymptotic mass represents the maximum recorded body condition for the species, typically achieved by older specimens. In contrast, an individual just reaching puberty will have a considerably lower body mass. The wet weight at puberty for this species is estimated at 29.5 grams [Wwp = 29.5 grams], which corresponds to the body mass expected for a fish of the pubertal length. This represents a critical energetic threshold, as the animal must allocate sufficient resources to both continued somatic growth and the initiation of reproductive activities. The tenfold increase in mass from maturity to the maximum size underscores a growth trajectory that continues well after the onset of reproduction.

Longevity records for the Sompat grunt indicate a maximum lifespan that can extend to 10 years [am = can extend to 10 years] at the average water temperature of approximately 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C], a duration that is comparatively long for a tropical lutjaniform fish of its ultimate body size. This lifespan estimate comes from captive rearing studies and otolith-based age readings from wild populations. The relatively extended period of life allows for multiple spawning seasons, contributing to the species' overall reproductive output across its lifetime. A ten-year lifespan provides ample opportunity for iteroparous reproduction, enabling individual fish to buffer against years of poor recruitment. Reproductive senility is not commonly observed in this species, though a gradual decline in fecundity with age has been noted in some older individuals. The combination of early maturation and a lengthy adult phase is a life history strategy well suited to the relatively stable, food-rich environments of the Gulf of Guinea.

Reproduction in the Sompat grunt is characterized by a distinct spawning strategy that aligns with seasonal productivity cycles in its coastal habitat. From a reproductive standpoint, the species is iteroparous and exhibits group-synchronous oocyte development. Ecological observations suggest that a single gravid female may release between 150,000 and 250,000 pelagic eggs per spawning event, with a typical female participating in one to two such events annually. This high fecundity, combined with the small egg size and brief incubation period, results in a prodigious larval output that helps offset high early-life mortality. The eggs are buoyant and drift with the currents, facilitating dispersal. Spawning appears to be timed with peak zooplankton abundance to maximize larval feeding success, a pattern observed in many congeneric species within the region. The trade-off between numerous small offspring and the minimal parental investment is a classic r-selected strategy within a largely demersal adult existence.
